current_behavior: 0/15 companies scored across all three dimensions, despite Shopify having clean, real, dated two-point evidence (merchant count 20,000 -> 80,000 over ~3 years) that a human analyst could defensibly convert into a growth-rate figure.
tier_discrimination_problem: Total non-discrimination -- these three dimensions contribute nothing to any of the 15 companies' scores, in the one pillar (Traction) explicitly intended to carry the hardest, most objective evidence in the whole methodology.
problem_type: Pure thresholding/conversion-function absence, not scale placement or compression. The evidence itself is fine where it exists; there is simply no function to turn a growth rate into a 0-10 score.
evidence_needed_to_calibrate: A materiality floor, a business-model-aware comparison window, and a rate-to-score conversion table -- calibrated against a broader sample of real growth-rate/quality-outcome pairs than the single clean case (Shopify) this portfolio can support alone. This is a single high-leverage fix: solving it once likely unlocks all three dimensions at once, since they share the same missing conversion-function root cause.

current_behavior: 7 of 15 companies have real, family-appropriate qualitative or partial-quantitative evidence (Beepi's disclosed 9% marketplace take-rate, Oscar Health's disclosed underwriting losses, Warby Parker's DTC value-chain-compression thesis, Ginkgo's R&D-partnership model) that is completely blocked from producing a score.
tier_discrimination_problem: Financial Health showed the SHARPEST discrimination of any pillar wherever it was actually available in this PASS (range 1.55-7.0, versus e.g. Market's compressed 4.0-6.75) -- unblocking these 7 companies would likely both raise Financial Health coverage from 33% toward 80%+ AND meaningfully sharpen portfolio-wide discrimination.
problem_type: Pure anchor/threshold absence (real evidence exists, conversion missing), not compression.
evidence_needed_to_calibrate: Comparable companies' disclosed take-rates (marketplace), loss/combined ratios (insurance), and per-unit margins (hardware/DTC) at various stages, to establish family-specific 'what counts as good' thresholds. Requires a broader, family-specific benchmark sample beyond these 7 companies to avoid overfitting the anchor to this portfolio.

mode: Hybrid (just changed from Deterministic in the prior spec repair)
current_behavior: Functioning directionally in this rerun (Tesla scored appropriately at the bottom, Stripe appropriately positive), but every qualitative score assigned (Tesla=1, Oscar Health=3, Quibi=3, Stripe=7) reflects unaided single-analyst judgment against no FROZEN severity band.
tier_discrimination_problem: Not a coverage or compression problem -- a placement-consistency problem. A different analyst scoring the same Tesla evidence might reasonably land on a 1, 2, or 3; there is currently no way to check.
problem_type: Scale-placement/thresholding ambiguity -- newly introduced by enabling qualitative scoring at all, and worth being honest about rather than treating the numbers produced in this rerun as more precise than they are.
evidence_needed_to_calibrate: Qualitative severity-band definitions (what specific evidence pattern constitutes a 1 vs. a 3 vs. a 5) validated against either multiple independent analysts scoring the same evidence, or a larger sample of historical financial-crisis/health cases than this portfolio's single severe case (Tesla) can support.
